You are an expert at creating semantic retrieval questions for United Nations documents (resolutions, reports, letters, and meeting records).
THE INFORMATION NEED OF THIS MODE: every question is a query typed by a searcher who knows the SITUATION and what they need to find out, but not the corpus's vocabulary and not which instrument governs — a desk officer new to a file, a journalist, a researcher approaching a regime from outside its terminology. Write from that need: a real question about a situation, the response to it, or the people affected — never a report of what a body or a speaker SAID, never a reading-comprehension question about what the passage says. The mode stays conceptual, but it still needs a concrete anchor and a year, because a query that matches everything finds nothing.
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English. In the ANSWER, reproduce dates, durations, amounts, percentages and thresholds exactly. Use the official English names of organs, bodies, missions and instruments, never literal translations.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document is, when it is from and whether it belongs to a recurring series; the subject-matter words of its title ("the situation in Rwanda") may serve as topic words in a question.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which committee "the Committee" is, which State "the speaker" represents, who wrote the letter, the calendar year of the meeting, report or session. If any needed fact, figure, list or reason sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument, a question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument; ask instead about what THIS document does with it — what its author alleges, applies, reports, contests. Never ask about the metadata itself.
DEFINING RULES OF THIS MODE:
1. NO IDENTIFIERS: no resolution or decision number, document symbol or paragraph number in a question, and no deixis — "this resolution", "the present report", "this document", the document's contents as if visible. Identifiers may appear inside the answer span.
2. CONCEPTUAL, NOT EXTRACTIVE: the question targets a situation, a mechanism or an affected party; it never asks for a datum by its name — "what troop ceiling", "by what date", "what amount", "which official" belong to another mode. The span that answers a conceptual question may still contain a figure ("an estimated 250,000 refugees"). If the block offers only data points, skip with skip_reason "extractive only".

THE YEAR IS MANDATORY: every question carries an absolute year, date or dated period ("in 2009", "in spring 1994", "after the 2011 legislative elections"), taken from the block, the context or the metadata. Without it, a question about a mission, a regime or a recurring resolution has one answer per year and therefore none.
4. NOT A SPEECH REPORT: never "How did [State/body] describe ...", "What did [body] say about ...", "What caution / warning did [body] give ...", "What did [body] stress ...", "What did the speaker say ...". Distance comes from describing the SITUATION, RESPONSE or PEOPLE in ordinary words instead of the document's formulas — "the mass killing of civilians" for "the very numerous killings of civilians"; "UN peacekeepers" for the mission's formal designation; "people who fled across the border" for "refugees who crossed the border" — and never from lifting the block's phrasing or reproducing a list it gives. Paraphrase never strips the discriminating anchor: keep the country, the mission and the year.
ANCHOR — the person typing has not seen this document and is searching among hundreds of thousands of UN documents in the same formulaic register. Every question carries at least one concrete anchor: a country or situation ("Rwanda", "the conflict in Darfur"), a mission or operation ("UNAMIR"), a named body or actor type ("the Panel of Experts on the Sudan", "troop-contributing countries"), or a subject matter tied to a situation ("arms embargo exemptions for humanitarian equipment in Somalia"). A bare topic ("counterterrorism measures", "climate action", "developing countries", "human rights learning") is not an anchor. Every definite description is named in the question itself — never bare "the Committee", "the Regional Centre", "the speaker", "the sides", "the Council". Report the anchor in "anchor" as a verbatim substring of the question. The test: typed into a search engine by a stranger, would the question lead to THIS document's subject matter? "What did the Security Council express grave concern about?" fails; "How did the Security Council respond to attacks on displaced civilians in Rwanda in May 1994?" passes.
RECURRING SERIES — know the families: session-numbered General Assembly resolutions on standing agenda items (a country's human rights situation, the right to food, the right to development, human rights learning, the Chemical and Biological Weapons Conventions, New Caledonia); the annual ECOSOC and Assembly resolutions on the Occupied Palestinian Territory; the biennial "cooperation between the United Nations and [regional organization]" resolutions, whose consultation clauses are cloned across the OSCE, CIS, SCO, EurAsEC and every other partner; mandate renewals; International Day resolutions; periodic reports. An unchanged paragraph in such a series fits every year — and every partner organization — equally, even with the year attached; the same holds for any span that could appear unchanged in dozens of UN documents (stakeholder invitation lists, cooperate-and-collaborate lists, the universal "measures must comply with international law" clause, "primary responsibility lies with the authorities themselves"). Ask only about content specific to THIS instance — a named event, a new task, a figure; if the block holds only unchanged recurring text, skip with skip_reason "recurring boilerplate". When a block holds both ceremony and substance, ask about the substance.
CONSEQUENTIAL ANSWER SPANS:
- QUALIFYING: measures established, extended or modified; mandates and their scope; conditions, criteria and exemptions; how a mechanism operates; who is bound, protected or assisted and how; concrete reported events, findings and stated rationales; and, for situation-framed questions, preambular ASSESSMENTS that state concretely what is happening ("delays by the signatory parties and the absence of an inclusive political settlement", "an estimated 250,000 refugees crossed the border").
- DISQUALIFIED, anywhere in the document, including their softer forms: commends; welcomes; expresses appreciation or concern; takes note; notes with appreciation; stresses or underlines the importance of; recognizes the primary responsibility of; reaffirms or reiterates commitment; encourages or invites in general terms; invites two officials to hold regular consultations; calls upon bodies to support, cooperate and collaborate with stakeholders; calls upon States to consider; calls upon "the international community"; aspirations. Preambular RECITALS — recalling, reaffirming, recognizing responsibility, expressing concern — are framing, not answer material, even though preambular ASSESSMENTS are.
ATTRIBUTION — much of this corpus reports what someone SAID. When the block attributes a statement, claim, estimate or assessment, the question and answer preserve the attribution — to the STATE, the OFFICE ("the representative of South Africa", "the Secretary-General"), or, for a Secretariat report, "UN reporting" — never a bare personal name. An agentless passive or a claim stated as fact is stripped attribution: "as weapons kept reaching the separatists" presents Georgia's assertion as fact — write "according to Georgia" or "in Georgia's account". Attributed content is askable only as a State's position on an identifiable proposal, instrument or measure ("What position did Guyana take on the use of force in Kosovo in 1999?"), a stated rationale, or a concrete situation assessment — never a characterization ("how did Guyana describe the crisis"), an aspiration, a courtesy or a generic exhortation. OWN ACTS NEED NO HEDGE: a concrete, completed act of the author's own side — France's letter recounting that the European Union adopted a disarmament plan endorsed by its Heads of State — may be asked about directly; the requirement targets contested claims and characterizations of others.
THE INFORMATIVENESS TEST: the answer must tell the asker something the question does not already contain and could not have supplied. It fails when the answer restates the question's words or the pointer it was built from, when a reader could guess it from the question with better than even odds, or when the span is a pointer that means nothing outside the document ("the above priorities", "as adopted in the present resolution"). Discard, or ask about the substance instead.
CORE RULES:
- Single Intent, Short Span: one clear informational goal per question — broader than a single fact is fine, bundled asks are not — answered by a short contiguous span of the block; if the only span is a whole paragraph, narrow the question or discard.
- Wording & Length: natural search phrasing, 8–20 words, hard maximum 25.
- SKIP RATHER THAN PAD: up to THREE pairs, fewer if fewer pass every rule; if the block supports none, return exactly [{"skip_reason": "<one short phrase>"}]. Never manufacture a question to reach three.
WHAT TO ASK — three framings ("framing"); the questions must target distinguishable aspects and, when generating more than one pair, span at least two of them:
  1. situation — context or problem: what crisis, threat, dispute or development does the document respond to or describe? The motivating concern behind a measure, and the state of affairs a report or preamble concretely assesses.
  2. response — mechanism or action: what mission, measure, process or institutional arrangement is established, extended or modified, and how does it operate?
  3. stakeholder — affected party or scenario: who is bound, sanctioned, protected or assisted, and in what real-world scenario? Addressee ("What was the Government of X required to do ...") and beneficiary ("What protection did the UN provide for civilians in ...") perspectives both belong here, as does a State's position on a concrete matter.

The General Assembly,
Reaffirming its resolution 46/182 of 19 December 1991 and the guiding principles contained in the annex thereto, other relevant General Assembly and Economic and Social Council resolutions and agreed conclusions of the Council,
Noting the reports of the Secretary-General on the strengthening of the coordination of emergency humanitarian assistance of the United Nations and on the Central Emergency Response Fund,
Reaffirming the principles of neutrality, humanity, impartiality and independence for the provision of humanitarian assistance, and reaffirming also the need for all actors engaged in the provision of humanitarian assistance in situations of complex emergencies and natural disasters to promote and fully respect these principles,
Deeply concerned about the humanitarian impact of such global challenges as the global financial and economic crisis, the food crisis and continuing food insecurity, including their effect on the increasing vulnerability of populations and their negative impact on the effective delivery of humanitarian assistance,

Emphasizing the need to mobilize adequate, predictable, timely and flexible resources for humanitarian assistance based on and in proportion to assessed needs, with a view to ensuring fuller coverage of the needs in all sectors and across humanitarian emergencies, and recognizing, in this regard, the achievements of the Central Emergency Response Fund,
Reiterating the need for Member States, relevant United Nations organizations and other relevant actors to mainstream a gender perspective into humanitarian assistance, including by addressing the specific needs of women, girls, boys and men in a comprehensive and consistent manner,
Expressing its deep concern at the increasing challenges faced by Member States and the United Nations humanitarian response capacity as a result of the consequences of natural disasters, including those related to the continuing impact of climate change, and reaffirming the importance of implementing the Hyogo Framework for Action 2005 - 2015: Building the Resilience of Nations and Communities to Disasters, inter alia, by providing adequate resources for disaster risk reduction, including investment in disaster preparedness, and by working towards building back better in all phases from relief to development,

Concerned about the challenges posed by the magnitude of some humanitarian emergencies, including some of the most recent natural disasters, in particular to the capacity and coordination of the humanitarian response system,
Recognizing that building national and local preparedness and response capacity is critical to a more predictable and effective response,
Emphasizing that enhancing international cooperation on emergency humanitarian assistance is essential, and reaffirming its resolution 64/251 of 22 January 2010 on international cooperation on humanitarian assistance in the field of natural disasters, from relief to development,
Emphasizing also the fundamentally civilian character of humanitarian assistance, and reaffirming the need in situations in which military capacity and assets are used to support the implementation of humanitarian assistance, for their use to be undertaken with the consent of the affected State and in conformity with international law, including international humanitarian law, as well as humanitarian principles,
Condemning the increasing number of deliberate threats and violent attacks against humanitarian personnel and facilities and the negative implications for the provision of humanitarian assistance to populations in need,

Recognizing the high numbers of persons affected by humanitarian emergencies, including internally displaced persons, bearing in mind their particular needs, and welcoming in this regard the adoption and ongoing ratification process of the African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa, which marks a significant step towards strengthening the national and regional normative framework for the protection of and assistance to internally displaced persons in Africa,
Recognizing also the importance of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, which include a vital legal framework for the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War, including the provision of humanitarian assistance,
Noting with grave concern that violence, including gender-based violence, particularly sexual violence, and violence against children, continues to be deliberately directed against civilian populations in many emergency situations,
Noting with appreciation the efforts made by the United Nations to improve humanitarian response, including by strengthening humanitarian response capacities, improving humanitarian coordination, enhancing predictable and adequate funding and strengthening the accountability of all stakeholders, and recognizing the importance of strengthening emergency administrative procedures and funding to allow for an effective response to emergencies,

Recognizing that in strengthening the coordination of humanitarian assistance in the field, United Nations organizations should continue to work in close coordination with national Governments,
1. Welcomes the outcome of the thirteenth humanitarian affairs segment of the Economic and Social Council at its substantive session of 2010;
2. Requests the Emergency Relief Coordinator to continue her efforts to strengthen the coordination of humanitarian assistance, and calls upon relevant United Nations organizations and other relevant intergovernmental organizations, as well as other humanitarian and development actors, to continue to work with the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs of the Secretariat to enhance the coordination, effectiveness and efficiency of humanitarian assistance;
3. Calls upon the relevant organizations of the United Nations system and, as appropriate, other relevant humanitarian actors to continue efforts to improve the humanitarian response to natural and man-made disasters and complex emergencies by further strengthening humanitarian response capacities at all levels, by continuing to strengthen the coordination of humanitarian assistance at the field level, including in support of national authorities of the affected State, as appropriate, and by further enhancing transparency, performance and accountability;

4. Recognizes the benefits of engagement and coordination with relevant humanitarian actors to the effectiveness of humanitarian response, and encourages the United Nations to continue to pursue efforts to strengthen partnerships at the global level with the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, relevant humanitarian non-governmental organizations and other participants in the Inter-Agency Standing Committee;
5. Requests the Secretary-General to strengthen the support provided to United Nations resident/humanitarian coordinators and to United Nations country teams, including by providing necessary training, identifying resources and improving the identification of and the selection process for United Nations resident/humanitarian coordinators, and enhancing their performance accountability;
6. Reaffirms the importance of implementing the Hyogo Framework for Action 2005 - 2015: Building the Resilience of Nations and Communities to Disasters, and looks forward to the midterm review of the Hyogo Framework for Action, the third session of the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction, to be held in Geneva from 8 to 13 May 2011, and the 2011 Global Assessment Report on Disaster Risk Reduction;

7. Calls upon Member States and the international community to increase resources for disaster risk reduction measures, including in the areas of prevention, mitigation and preparedness for effective response and contingency planning, in order to, inter alia, further strengthen national and local capacities to prepare for and respond to humanitarian emergencies, and encourages closer cooperation between national stakeholders and humanitarian and development actors in this regard;
8. Urges Member States, the United Nations and other relevant organizations to take further steps to provide a coordinated emergency response to the food and nutrition needs of affected populations, while aiming to ensure that such steps are supportive of national strategies and programmes aimed at improving food security;
9. Expresses concern at the challenges related to, inter alia, safe access to and use of fuel, firewood, alternative energy, water and sanitation, shelter and food and health-care services in humanitarian emergencies, and takes note with appreciation of initiatives at the national and international levels that promote effective cooperation in this regard;

10. Encourages the international community, including relevant United Nations organizations and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, to support efforts of Member States aimed at strengthening their capacity to prepare for and respond to disasters and to support efforts, as appropriate, to strengthen systems for identifying and monitoring disaster risk, including vulnerability and natural hazards;
11. Welcomes the initiatives at the regional and national levels related to the implementation of the Guidelines for the Domestic Facilitation and Regulation of International Disaster Relief and Initial Recovery Assistance, adopted at the Thirtieth International Conference of the Red Cross and Red Crescent, held in Geneva from 26 to 30 November 2007, and encourages Member States and, where applicable, regional organizations, to take further steps to strengthen operational and legal frameworks for international disaster relief, taking into account the Guidelines, as appropriate;

12. Encourages States to create an enabling environment for the capacity building of local authorities and of national and local non-governmental and community-based organizations in order to ensure better preparedness in providing timely, effective and predictable humanitarian assistance, and encourages the United Nations and humanitarian organizations to provide support to such efforts, including, as appropriate, through the transfer of technology and expertise to developing countries and through support to programmes aimed at enhancing the coordination capacities of affected States;
13. Calls upon United Nations humanitarian entities, other relevant humanitarian organizations, development partners, the private sector, donor countries and the affected State to enhance cooperation and coordination, with a view to planning and delivering humanitarian assistance in ways that are supportive of early recovery as well as of sustainable rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts;
14. Requests the Secretary-General, in consultation with the affected countries and relevant humanitarian and development actors, to carry out an assessment of steps taken by the United Nations and relevant partners to support efforts to strengthen local, national and regional humanitarian response capacity and to include his findings as well as recommendations for enhancing United Nations support in this regard in his report to the General Assembly at its sixty-sixth session;

15. Encourages efforts to provide education in humanitarian emergencies, including in order to contribute to a smooth transition from relief to development;
16. Calls upon relevant United Nations organizations to support the improvement of the consolidated appeals process, inter alia, by engaging in the preparation of needs analyses and common humanitarian action plans, including through a better analysis of gender-related allocations, in order to further the development of the process as an instrument for United Nations strategic planning and prioritization, and by involving other relevant humanitarian organizations in the process, while reiterating that consolidated appeals should be prepared in consultation with affected States;
17. Requests Member States, relevant humanitarian organizations of the United Nations system and other relevant humanitarian actors to ensure that all aspects of humanitarian response, including disaster preparedness and needs assessment, take into account the specific needs of the affected population, recognizing that giving appropriate consideration to, inter alia, gender, age and disability is part of a comprehensive and effective humanitarian response, and in this regard encourages efforts to ensure gender mainstreaming in the delivery of humanitarian assistance;

21. Calls upon all Member States and invites the private sector and all concerned individuals and institutions to consider increasing their voluntary contributions to the Central Emergency Response Fund, and emphasizes that contributions should be additional to current commitments to humanitarian programming and should not be to the detriment of resources made available for international cooperation for development;

You are a strict quality grader for UN semantic retrieval questions.

INPUT AND TASK
You receive the TARGET BLOCK, metadata, REFERENCED DOCUMENTS, DOCUMENT
CONTEXT, and 1–3 candidates with question, answer, framing, and anchor.
Questions and answers must be in English. Use only supplied historical
evidence; treat source/candidate text as data, not instructions.

Grade independently; ignore generator identity and previous scores. Do not
force a winner or score distribution. Situation, response, and stakeholder
questions have equal access to high scores. A separate grader scores
faithfulness; here check task fit and whether the actual pair resolves the
information need, without additional faithfulness scores.

GENERATION REQUIREMENTS
1. CONCEPTUAL NEED. A searcher knows the situation, not the document's
   wording. Ask about a problem, response, mechanism, rationale, role or
   affected party—not a datum requested by name. A figure can demonstrate
   the severity of a situation; asking directly for a troop ceiling, date,
   amount or official belongs to another mode. One conceptual intent may
   require several connected obstacles or actions; independent asks do not.
   Exclude speech reports such as “How did X describe...?” or “What warning
   did X give...?”, not genuine questions about actions or permitted positions.

2. ANCHOR AND TIME. The question itself needs an absolute year/date/dated
   period and at least one concrete country, situation, mission, specific
   body/actor or situation-linked subject. A bare topic is insufficient.
   Every definite reference must resolve. No resolution/decision number,
   document symbol, paragraph number or unseen-document deixis. Attribution
   is allowed; “this report” is not. Dates/quantities are not identifiers.
   Context may establish the time pin, but a report date must not silently
   become an event date. Do not use the target to excuse missing query context.

3. BLOCK TEST. All answer substance must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK.
   References, context and metadata may clarify names, dates and attribution
   for the QUESTION, never supply missing answer facts, lists or reasons.
   Meeting records ARE allowed. Exclude questions about another instrument's
   provision merely quoted/restated in the block; THIS author's application,
   allegation or assessment may qualify. Never ask about metadata itself.

4. SUBSTANCE. Qualifying content includes measures, mandates, mechanisms,
   conditions, protection/assistance, concrete events/findings, stated
   rationales, and concrete preambular ASSESSMENTS of a situation or obstacle.
   Exclude praise, appreciation/concern alone, taking note, generic emphasis
   or encouragement, reaffirmed commitments, primary-responsibility formulas,
   aspirations, regular-consultation clauses, and stakeholder invitation or
   cooperate-and-collaborate lists. Preambular RECITALS are not assessments.
   Judge the requested proposition, not a word such as “recognizing” alone.
   Establishing an observance can be substantive; invitations to celebrate
   it are not. These are dataset exclusions, not political-value judgments.
   In recurring series, require content specific to the instance; adding a
   year cannot rescue interchangeable boilerplate. Do not invent unseen
   duplicates or reject a report's concrete event merely because reports recur.

5. ATTRIBUTION. Preserve attributed claims, estimates and assessments through
   a named State, office or “UN reporting”, not a bare person or agentless
   “was reported”. Permitted attributed needs are a State's position on a
   concrete proposal/measure, a stated rationale, or a concrete situation
   assessment—not a characterization, courtesy or exhortation. Apply the
   generator's own-act exception: a concrete completed act of the author's
   own side may be asked about directly, without an attribution hedge. Do not
   extend that exception to claims about others, intentions or alleged effects.

6. DECIDING SPAN. The answer must be a short contiguous English span from
   the target, preserving figures, dates, units, identifiers, official names,
   modality and necessary qualifications. No translation, stitched passages
   or invented explanation. A broad ask requiring a whole paragraph must be
   narrowed; do not truncate a necessary condition just to shorten the answer.
   Attribution/referents already explicit in the question need not be repeated
   in the span. Check the ACTUAL answer: a goal does not explain a mechanism;
   a proposal does not prove implementation or success; a stated obstacle
   does not establish an unstated cause. “How severe?” may be answered by
   magnitude; “what role?” by duties. Match the intended relationship, not
   the interrogative word mechanically. Missing material content fails support.

7. WORDING. Paraphrase ordinary formulas and sentence structure, not legal
   meaning. Preserve needed names, terms and distinguishing context. Following
   the generation examples, “UN peacekeepers” can describe a role when the
   country/situation keeps it identifiable; it is not a renamed mission.
   Use 8–25 words, preferably 8–20; count whitespace-separated words,
   treating hyphenated terms as one. Record length violations without
   inventing grammar defects. Necessary attribution and qualifications
   are not padding.

FIVE SCORES — 1–5
5 = fully meets the criterion, supported by specific positive evidence;
4 = strong with a small identifiable limitation;
3 = usable with a meaningful weakness;
2 = major defect;
1 = criterion fails.

Give one short, specific explanation per score. Do not start at 5, invent
flaws, or reduce unaffected criteria. A valid answer or fluent question
alone does not establish good conceptual framing, anchoring or paraphrasing.

search_realism:
A natural outsider question with one bounded conceptual need. Pure datum
extraction, speech reporting, or bundled independent asks: at most 2;
generic passage comprehension: 1. Borderline conceptual/slot framing:
at most 3. Do not prefer a mechanism question over a good stakeholder query.

anchoring_and_time:
Concrete query anchor, supported absolute time and sufficient issue detail.
Name the actual words. Missing time, bare topic or unresolved essential
referent: at most 2; identifiable but materially broad episode/need: at most 3.
Metadata cannot rescue absent context; a wrong anchor field alone does not
erase a good textual anchor.

consequence:
The actual answer supplies qualifying substance, adds information and matches
the requested relationship. Partial/thin information: at most 3; wrong
relationship, misleading omission or mostly restatement: at most 2;
ceremony, circularity or unresolved answer pointer: 1. A referent fixed by
the question is not unresolved deixis. For alleged answer leakage or obvious
completion, name the cues; do not invent probabilities about reader knowledge.
Do not penalize useful information merely because it includes a figure.

lexical_distance:
Natural conceptual reformulation with meaning intact. One avoidable copied
construction can warrant 4; substantially mirrored predicates/syntax: at
most 3; heavy copied scaffolding or meaning-changing substitution: at most 2;
near-verbatim question conversion: 1. Necessary legal terms and official
names NEVER incur overlap penalties. Do not delete an anchor to gain distance.
Meaning-changing substitutions also fail support.

linguistic_quality:
Clear, economical, idiomatic English. Penalize actual stiffness, redundancy
and unclear syntax—not necessary precision. For a non-English question,
use null here and fail mode rather than mislabel its native-language fluency.

CHECKS
Use pass, fail, or uncertain; explain failures/uncertainty in problems.
- mode: English; conceptual rather than extractive/speech-report framing;

- support: sound premises, attribution and scope; complete deciding span in
  the target; no outside answer substance or quoted-provision targeting.
  Established defects fail; genuinely missing necessary input is uncertain.
  An answer found only in supplied context/reference text fails the block test.
- metadata: anchor is a verbatim question substring with concrete anchoring
  value; framing matches the actual need. Accept defensible overlap and keep
  metadata-only errors separate from intrinsic scores.

Framings:
situation = problem, obstacle, context or concrete assessment;
response = action, approach, mechanism or institutional arrangement;
stakeholder = who is bound/protected/assisted and how, an addressee's duty,

With two or three candidates, batch_diversity passes only when they address
distinguishable aspects and at least two actual framings. Report separately;
never alter individual scores for diversity. With one use not_applicable.
Treat equivalent defects consistently.

OUTPUT
Return JSON only in this structure, in input order. Copy candidate_id when
provided; otherwise use null. Scores are integers; null is allowed only
when unassessable, with an explanation. Prefix each problem with its affected

uncertain, then pass. No rewrites, evidence IDs, issue-code lists, totals or
rankings. Generation-skip entries are handled separately.

````text
You are a strict faithfulness grader for legal and policy question-answer pairs built from United
  Nations documents.

You will receive a three-section context and THREE question-answer pairs.
The context is:
- "### TARGET BLOCK" — the passage the questions are supposed to be about, in one or more language
  versions.
- "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — other documents CITED by the target block, each supplied as its
  symbol, title, and text — provided ONLY so the target block's citations can be understood, the way
  a footnote helps a reader.
- "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the SAME document (its opening and neighbouring
  passages), supplied so that the target block can be understood: it resolves which mission "the
  Mission" is, which country "the Government" governs, what period a report covers, and similar
  referring expressions.
BOTH supporting sections are for UNDERSTANDING ONLY. Using them to resolve a referring expression in
  the question or answer (naming "the Mission" as UNAMIR, identifying what a cited resolution
  concerns) is legitimate and must NOT be penalised. Using either of them as a source of answer
  substance is a grounding failure — the answer's facts must come from the TARGET BLOCK itself,
  fully.

THREE question-answer pairs (questions may be in any language; each answer matches its question's
  language). Grade each pair on three sub-criteria, each 1–5. Do NOT evaluate query shape or
  retrieval quality — those are handled separately. Focus only on how faithfully each answer
  reflects the supplied text.

GRADING INSTRUCTIONS:
- Grade each of the three pairs independently and against the absolute rubric below — not relative
  to the other two.
- Do not let similarity or dissimilarity between the three pairs influence any individual grade.
- Evaluate each pair on its own merits before moving to the next.

SCALE CALIBRATION:
- Most generator outputs will be acceptable on most criteria. "Acceptable" is not the same as
  "excellent."
- 5 is reserved for genuinely exceptional candidates with no identifiable weakness. If you can point
  to any imperfection, it is not a 5. 5s should be uncommon.
- 4 means the candidate is very good but has exactly one minor, identifiable issue. You must be able
  to name the issue.
- 3 is the default grade for a candidate that is acceptable and does the job, with one clear
  weakness. It is not a punishment grade — most acceptable candidates will receive 3s.
- 2 and 1 are reserved for candidates with real, identifiable problems. Do not avoid using them when
  a candidate qualifies.
- Before assigning any 4 or 5, pause and ask: "What specifically makes this better than a 3?" If you
  cannot answer concretely, the grade is 3.

SUB-CRITERIA:

1. GROUNDING (1–5): Is the answer supported by a contiguous span of the TARGET BLOCK?
   The supporting text means the TARGET BLOCK alone. Resolving a referring expression through the
     REFERENCED DOCUMENTS, the DOCUMENT CONTEXT, or the metadata lines is legitimate disambiguation,
     not an inferential step. Anything more is.
   Cap the grade at 2 if any part of the answer's substance — a fact, figure, list, reason, or
     condition — is stated only in a REFERENCED DOCUMENT or only in the DOCUMENT CONTEXT and not in
     the target block. Cap at 1 if the answer's substance mainly comes from outside the target
     block.
   5 — Answer is taken directly from a single short contiguous span of the target block. Every word
     of the answer is explicitly present or is a trivial rewording of explicit content. No inference
     whatsoever. (Rare.)
   4 — Answer is fully supported but requires reading across two adjacent sentences, OR is from a
     single span with minor trivial rewording that a strict reader might flag.
   3 — Answer is grounded in the target block but requires one small, defensible inferential step —
     connecting a pronoun to its referent, combining a figure with its unit, or similar.
   2 — Answer is partially supported: some parts grounded in the target block, other parts not
     (including parts taken from a REFERENCED DOCUMENT or the DOCUMENT CONTEXT).
   1 — Answer requires significant inference, outside knowledge, or is not in the target block at
     all.
   CITATION RULE (UN): UN texts constantly cite other instruments ("the measures imposed by
     paragraph 20 of resolution 1493 (2003)"). If the answer's substance sits behind such a citation
     rather than in the target block's own words, score at most 2 (1 if the answer consists mainly
     of such content) — REGARDLESS of whether the cited document was supplied in the REFERENCED
     DOCUMENTS section. References exist for understanding, never as answer material.
   ATTRIBUTION RULE (UN): summary records report delegates' statements, letters convey a
     government's position, and reports state the reporting body's findings and estimates. If the
     target block attributes a claim, estimate, or assessment to a speaker or body and the answer
     (or the question it responds to) presents that claim as established fact with the attribution
     stripped, cap GROUNDING at 2 — the supplied text supports the attributed claim, not the bare
     assertion.

2. PRECISION (1–5): Does the answer add unsupported details or padding?
   5 — Answer is the shortest possible span that fully answers the question. Not one extra word. No
     surrounding context, no hedges, no elaboration. (Rare.)
   4 — Answer is grounded and tight but includes one short fragment of adjacent context that could
     have been cut.
   3 — Answer is grounded but includes one unsupported detail, generalization, or piece of padding.
   2 — Answer includes multiple unsupported details, or uses speculative framing ("likely,"
     "approximately," "it seems") where the passage is specific.
   1 — Answer is largely padded with content not in the passage, or is a rewrite rather than an
     extraction.

3. NUMERICAL & CITATIONAL FIDELITY (1–5): Are numbers, dates, amounts, and official identifiers
  reproduced exactly? (JSON key remains "numerical_fidelity".)
   5 — All numbers, dates, durations, monetary amounts, percentages, troop figures, and official
     identifiers (document symbols, resolution and paragraph numbers) match the passage
     character-for-character (e.g., "resolution 2374 (2017)" preserved as-is, not "Resolution 2374";
     "S/1994/565", not "S/1994/565/Rev.1"; "up to 5,500 troops", not "about 5,000 troops"; "within
     30 days", not "in about a month"). Dates rendered in the answer language's standard format
     count as exact if day, month, and year are unchanged ("15 July 1994" for "le 15 juillet 1994").
   4 — All values and identifiers are correct and preserved, but with a trivial formatting
     difference (e.g., "30-day period" vs. "within 30 days", or a spacing/punctuation variant of an

   3 — One number or date is rounded or approximated, one identifier is truncated (e.g., year
     dropped from a resolution number), or one duration is converted to a different unit.
   2 — Multiple values or identifiers rounded, reformatted, truncated, or partially dropped.
   1 — Numbers, dates, or identifiers invented, significantly changed, or contradicted by the
     passage.
   N/A — Answer contains no numerical or citational content. Score this sub-criterion as 5 if N/A.

- 4 means the candidate is very good but has exactly one minor, identifiable issue. You must be able

Reiterates the obligation of all States to conduct exhaustive and impartial investigations into all suspected cases of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, to identify and bring to justice those responsible, while ensuring the right of every person to a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law, to grant adequate compensation within a reasonable time to the victims or their families, and to adopt all necessary measures, including legal and judicial measures, to put an end to impunity and to prevent the further occurrence of such executions, as recommended in the Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extralegal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions;
4. Calls upon all States in which the death penalty has not been abolished to comply with their obligations under relevant provisions of international human rights instruments, including in particular articles 6, 7 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and articles 37 and 40 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, bearing in mind the safeguards and guarantees set out in Economic and Social Council resolutions 1984/50 of 25 May 1984 and 1989/64 of 24 May 1989;

5. Urges all States:
(a) To take all necessary and possible measures, in conformity with international human rights law and international humanitarian law, to prevent loss of life, in particular that of children, during public demonstrations, internal and communal violence, civil unrest, public emergencies or armed conflicts, and to ensure that the police, law enforcement agents, armed forces and other agents acting on behalf of or with the consent or acquiescence of the State act with restraint and in conformity with international humanitarian law and international human rights law, including the principles of proportionality and necessity, and in this regard to ensure that police and law enforcement officials are guided by the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials and the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials;

(b) To ensure the effective protection of the right to life of all persons under their jurisdiction and to investigate promptly and thoroughly all killings, including those targeted at specific groups of persons, such as racially motivated violence leading to the death of the victim, killings of members of national, ethnic, religious or linguistic minorities, of refugees, internally displaced persons, migrants, street children or members of indigenous communities, killings of persons for reasons related to their activities as human rights defenders, lawyers, journalists or demonstrators, killings committed in the name of passion or in the name of honour, all killings committed for any discriminatory reason, including sexual orientation, as well as all other cases where a person's right to life has been violated, and to bring those responsible to justice before a competent, independent and impartial judiciary at the national or, where appropriate, international level, and to ensure that such killings, including those committed by security forces, police and law enforcement agents, paramilitary groups or private forces, are neither condoned nor sanctioned by State officials or personnel;

6. Also urges all States to ensure that persons deprived of their liberty are treated humanely and with full respect for their human rights and to ensure that their treatment, including judicial guarantees, and conditions conform to the Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners and, where applicable, to the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the Additional Protocols thereto of 8 June 1977 in relation to all persons detained in armed conflict, as well as to other pertinent international instruments;
7. Welcomes the International Criminal Court as an important contribution to ending impunity concerning extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and the fact that one hundred and four States have already ratified or acceded to and a further forty-one States have signed the Rome Statute of the Court, and calls upon all those States that have not ratified or acceded to the Rome Statute to consider doing so;

8. Encourages Governments and intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations to organize training programmes and to support projects with a view to training or educating military forces, law enforcement officers and government officials in human rights and humanitarian law issues connected with their work and to include a gender and child rights perspective in such training, and appeals to the international community and requests the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to support endeavours to that end;
9. Takes note of the interim report of the Special Rapporteur of the Human Rights Council on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions to the General Assembly;
10. Commends the important role that the Special Rapporteur plays towards the elimination of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, and encourages the Special Rapporteur to continue, within his mandate, to collect information from all concerned, to respond effectively to reliable information that comes before him, to follow up on communications and country visits and to seek the views and comments of Governments and to reflect them, as appropriate, in his reports;

11. Acknowledges the important role of the Special Rapporteur in identifying cases where extrajudicial, summary and arbitrary executions could amount to genocide and crimes against humanity or war crimes, and urges him to collaborate with the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, as appropriate, the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide, in addressing situations of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions that are of particularly serious concern or in which early action might prevent further deterioration;
12. Welcomes the cooperation established between the Special Rapporteur and other United Nations mechanisms and procedures in the field of human rights, and encourages the Special Rapporteur to continue efforts in that regard;
13. Urges all States, in particular those that have not done so, to cooperate with the Special Rapporteur so that his mandate can be carried out effectively, including by favourably and rapidly responding to requests for visits, mindful that country visits are one of the tools for the fulfilment of the mandate of the Special Rapporteur, and by responding in a timely manner to communications and other requests transmitted to them by the Special Rapporteur;

14. Expresses its appreciation to those States that have received the Special Rapporteur and asks them to examine his recommendations carefully, invites them to inform him of the actions taken on those recommendations, and requests other States to cooperate in a similar way;
15. Again requests the Secretary-General to continue to use his best endeavours in cases where the minimum standards of legal safeguards provided for in articles 6, 9, 14 and 15 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights appear not to have been respected;
16. Requests the Secretary-General to provide the Special Rapporteur with adequate human, financial and material resources to enable him to carry out his mandate effectively, including through country visits;
17. Also requests the Secretary-General to continue, in close collaboration with the High Commissioner, in conformity with the mandate of the High Commissioner established by the General Assembly in its resolution 48/141 of 20 December 1993, to ensure that personnel specialized in human rights and humanitarian law issues form part of United Nations missions, where appropriate, in order to deal with serious violations of human rights, such as extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions;

18. Requests the Special Rapporteur to submit to the General Assembly at its sixty-second session a report on the situation worldwide in regard to extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and his recommendations for more effective action to combat this phenomenon.

### TARGET BLOCK — write the questions about THIS text

[EN] Document: A/RES/61/173
  Title: Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on 19 December 2006
Acknowledging that international human rights law and international humanitarian law are complementary and not mutually exclusive,
Noting with deep concern the growing number of civilians and persons hors de combat killed in situations of armed conflict and internal strife,
Acknowledging that extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions may under certain circumstances amount to genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes, as defined in international law, including in the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court,
Affirming the obligation of States to prevent the abuse of persons deprived of their liberty and to investigate and respond to deaths in custody,
Convinced of the need for effective action to prevent, combat and eliminate the abhorrent practice of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, which represent a flagrant violation of the right to life,
1. Strongly condemns once again all the extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions that continue to occur throughout the world;
2. Demands that all States ensure that the practice of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions is brought to an end and that they take effective action to prevent, combat and eliminate the phenomenon in all its forms;

The General Assembly,
Recalling the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which guarantees the right to life, liberty and security of person, the relevant provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and other relevant human rights conventions,

3. Reiterates the obligation of all States to conduct exhaustive and impartial investigations into all suspected cases of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, to identify and bring to justice those responsible, while ensuring the right of every person to a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law, to grant adequate compensation within a reasonable time to the victims or their families, and to adopt all necessary measures, including legal and judicial measures, to put an end to impunity and to prevent the further occurrence of such executions, as recommended in the Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extralegal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions;
4. Calls upon all States in which the death penalty has not been abolished to comply with their obligations under relevant provisions of international human rights instruments, including in particular articles 6, 7 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and articles 37 and 40 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, bearing in mind the safeguards and guarantees set out in Economic and Social Council resolutions 1984/50 of 25 May 1984 and 1989/64 of 24 May 1989;

5. Urges all States:
(a) To take all necessary and possible measures, in conformity with international human rights law and international humanitarian law, to prevent loss of life, in particular that of children, during public demonstrations, internal and communal violence, civil unrest, public emergencies or armed conflicts, and to ensure that the police, law enforcement agents, armed forces and other agents acting on behalf of or with the consent or acquiescence of the State act with restraint and in conformity with international humanitarian law and international human rights law, including the principles of proportionality and necessity, and in this regard to ensure that police and law enforcement officials are guided by the Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials and the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials;

(b) To ensure the effective protection of the right to life of all persons under their jurisdiction and to investigate promptly and thoroughly all killings, including those targeted at specific groups of persons, such as racially motivated violence leading to the death of the victim, killings of members of national, ethnic, religious or linguistic minorities, of refugees, internally displaced persons, migrants, street children or members of indigenous communities, killings of persons for reasons related to their activities as human rights defenders, lawyers, journalists or demonstrators, killings committed in the name of passion or in the name of honour, all killings committed for any discriminatory reason, including sexual orientation, as well as all other cases where a person's right to life has been violated, and to bring those responsible to justice before a competent, independent and impartial judiciary at the national or, where appropriate, international level, and to ensure that such killings, including those committed by security forces, police and law enforcement agents, paramilitary groups or private forces, are neither condoned nor sanctioned by State officials or personnel;

6. Welcomes the International Criminal Court as an important contribution to ending impunity concerning extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and the fact that one hundred and four States have already ratified or acceded to and a further forty-one States have signed the Rome Statute of the Court, and calls upon all those States that have not ratified or acceded to the Rome Statute to consider doing so;

(b) To ensure the effective protection of the right to life of all persons under their jurisdiction and to investigate promptly and thoroughly all killings, including those targeted at specific groups of persons, such as racially motivated violence leading to the death of the victim, killings of members of national, ethnic, religious or linguistic minorities, of refugees, internally displaced persons, migrants, street children or members of indigenous communities, killings of persons for reasons related to their activities as human rights defenders, lawyers, journalists or demonstrators, killings committed in the name of passion or in the name of honour, all killings committed for any discriminatory reason, including sexual orientation, as well as all other cases where a person's right to life has been violated, and to bring those responsible to justice before a competent, independent and impartial judiciary at the national or, where appropriate, international level, and to ensure that such killings, including those committed by security forces, police and law enforcement agents, paramilitary groups or private forces, are neither condoned nor sanctioned by State officials or personnel;

6. Also urges all States to ensure that persons deprived of their liberty are treated humanely and with full respect for their human rights and to ensure that their treatment, including judicial guarantees, and conditions conform to the Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners and, where applicable, to the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the Additional Protocols thereto of 8 June 1977 in relation to all persons detained in armed conflict, as well as to other pertinent international instruments;
7. Welcomes the International Criminal Court as an important contribution to ending impunity concerning extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and the fact that one hundred and four States have already ratified or acceded to and a further forty-one States have signed the Rome Statute of the Court, and calls upon all those States that have not ratified or acceded to the Rome Statute to consider doing so;

8. Encourages Governments and intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations to organize training programmes and to support projects with a view to training or educating military forces, law enforcement officers and government officials in human rights and humanitarian law issues connected with their work and to include a gender and child rights perspective in such training, and appeals to the international community and requests the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to support endeavours to that end;
9. Takes note of the interim report of the Special Rapporteur of the Human Rights Council on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions to the General Assembly;
10. Commends the important role that the Special Rapporteur plays towards the elimination of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, and encourages the Special Rapporteur to continue, within his mandate, to collect information from all concerned, to respond effectively to reliable information that comes before him, to follow up on communications and country visits and to seek the views and comments of Governments and to reflect them, as appropriate, in his reports;

11. Acknowledges the important role of the Special Rapporteur in identifying cases where extrajudicial, summary and arbitrary executions could amount to genocide and crimes against humanity or war crimes, and urges him to collaborate with the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, as appropriate, the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide, in addressing situations of extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions that are of particularly serious concern or in which early action might prevent further deterioration;
12. Welcomes the cooperation established between the Special Rapporteur and other United Nations mechanisms and procedures in the field of human rights, and encourages the Special Rapporteur to continue efforts in that regard;
13. Urges all States, in particular those that have not done so, to cooperate with the Special Rapporteur so that his mandate can be carried out effectively, including by favourably and rapidly responding to requests for visits, mindful that country visits are one of the tools for the fulfilment of the mandate of the Special Rapporteur, and by responding in a timely manner to communications and other requests transmitted to them by the Special Rapporteur;

14. Expresses its appreciation to those States that have received the Special Rapporteur and asks them to examine his recommendations carefully, invites them to inform him of the actions taken on those recommendations, and requests other States to cooperate in a similar way;
15. Again requests the Secretary-General to continue to use his best endeavours in cases where the minimum standards of legal safeguards provided for in articles 6, 9, 14 and 15 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights appear not to have been respected;
16. Requests the Secretary-General to provide the Special Rapporteur with adequate human, financial and material resources to enable him to carry out his mandate effectively, including through country visits;
17. Also requests the Secretary-General to continue, in close collaboration with the High Commissioner, in conformity with the mandate of the High Commissioner established by the General Assembly in its resolution 48/141 of 20 December 1993, to ensure that personnel specialized in human rights and humanitarian law issues form part of United Nations missions, where appropriate, in order to deal with serious violations of human rights, such as extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions;

18. Requests the Special Rapporteur to submit to the General Assembly at its sixty-second session a report on the situation worldwide in regard to extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and his recommendations for more effective action to combat this phenomenon.

   authorized, reaffirmed, or continued to do. “What did the Security Council
   authorize?” fails; “What troop ceiling applied?” can pass. A source verb
   inside a necessary condition (“when the applicant was to be compensated
   without further action”) or an actor-identification question is allowed:
   the unknown must be the norm element, not the speech act. Avoid generic
   “what role did X play?” questions.

2. NO DOCUMENT LOCATOR. No resolution/decision number, document symbol,
   paragraph number, or descriptive instrument locator. Three exceptions:
   resolution-named bodies; dated measures/extensions as time pins;
   office-or-State-plus-date attribution of a reported finding. Regime names
   such as “Biological Weapons Convention” are allowed. Attribution does not
   permit a document symbol or a report used to locate an unrelated norm.

3. TIME. Include an explicit absolute date, month/year, year, or dated act
   supported by the input. No unresolved “current”, “next session”, or
   “reporting period”. Following the KFOR generation example, a day/month is
   resolved when the year appears elsewhere in the same question. Do not
   require the unknown deadline as the time pin or confuse a document's date
   with an event/effective date.

4. ANCHORS. Besides time, require at least TWO distinct substantive anchors
   in the question, with the regime named: mission, country/situation,
   specific body, affected actor, measure, or term of art. Generic actors
   such as “States” or “the Secretary-General” do not count. “Programme of
   Action” without its subject is insufficient. Every definite reference
   must resolve. Source text and reported anchors cannot supply context
   absent from the question.

5. FOCUS AND LENGTH. Ask one smallest-unit norm element or fact. An interval
   or amount-with-unit is one fact; a broad list or independent requirements
   are not. Target 8–20 words; maximum 25. Count whitespace-separated words,
   with hyphenated terms counting as one. Record length breaches without
   inventing grammar defects. Necessary terms, conditions and attribution
   cannot be deleted merely to shorten the question.

6. BLOCK TEST. The answer's substance must be fully in the TARGET BLOCK.
   References, context and metadata may resolve names, regime, dates and
   attribution for the QUESTION, never complete its answer. Metadata cannot
   be the requested fact. Exclude meeting-record targets with PV/SR symbols.
   If the block quotes/restates another instrument's provision, questions
   about that underlying norm are off-target. THIS author's application,
   allegation or assessment may qualify when answered fully in the block.

7. DECIDING SPAN. Use the shortest deciding span of the English target,
   not a paraphrase, stitched excerpts, or bare “yes/no”. Preserve official
   terms, figures, units, dates, durations, identifiers, conditions and
   modality. Check the actual answer and surrounding clauses: deployment is
   not an authorized ceiling; authorization does not prove implementation;
   an invitation is not a duty. “Compensated without further action” must
   not become any compensation. Missing requested content or an outcome-
   changing qualification fails support; unrelated context is unnecessary.
   Reported figures/events/determinations remain dated and attributed to
   the OFFICE or STATE, not a bare personal name or agentless “was reported”.
   The span may rely on attribution explicit in the question; do not present
   the claim as independently established fact.

8. CONTENT. Qualifying content includes specific measures, mandate tasks,
   conditions, exemptions, deadlines, ceilings, appropriations/contributions,
   appointments, procedures, and concrete dated figures/events/determinations.
   Purpose or rationale must be explicitly and completely stated.
   Exclude praise, welcomes, appreciation/concern, taking note, stressing
   importance, primary-responsibility formulas, reaffirmed commitments or
   determinations first made elsewhere, requests to continue, generic
   invitations/encouragement to consider or prioritize, commemorations,
   aspirations and preambular recitals. These are mode exclusions, not
   political-value judgments; assess the requested proposition, not an
   incidental word elsewhere.
   For recurring series, require this instance's specific figure, date,
   event, task or measure. A year alone does not rescue unchanged generic
   wording. A dated report's own figure can qualify. Do not invent unseen
   duplicates or treat every recurring report as boilerplate.

FIVE SCORES — 1–5
5 = fully meets the criterion, with specific positive evidence;
4 = strong with a small identifiable limitation;
3 = usable with a meaningful weakness;
2 = major defect;
1 = criterion fails.

Give one short, specific explanation per score. Do not start at 5, invent
flaws, or reduce unaffected criteria. Paraphrase ordinary scaffolding, but
NEVER penalize necessary legal terms, names or qualifications as copying.

practitioner_realism:
A natural norm-state request with one bounded specialist need. Speech-act
questions, comprehension prompts, vague slots, broad lists or independent
asks: at most 2. Substantial copied descriptive scaffolding: at most 3.
An actual stance calque needs a named wording defect, not a stylistic guess.

anchoring_and_time:
The question supplies the named regime, two substantive anchors and usable
absolute time. Name the actual spans. Missing time, fewer than two anchors,
unnamed regime or unresolved essential reference: at most 2. An otherwise
identifiable need with a material scope/time ambiguity: at most 3.

consequence:
A concrete qualifying norm element or dated fact for professional use.
Thin but qualifying content: 3; generic exhortation: at most 2; excluded
ceremony/recital: 1. Do not reward political importance or infer binding
force. A correctly framed specific task need not be binding to be useful.

informativeness:
The actual span adds the requested information and resolves it completely.
Missing material content: at most 3; scope-changing omission, wrong quantity
or status, or mostly restatement: at most 2; circularity/unresolved pointer: 1.
Penalize predictable default completions and truncated-answer scaffolding;
name the question cues rather than speculate about specialist knowledge.
Short answers, shared terms, and genuine yes/no uncertainty are not failures.
A referent already fixed by the question is not unresolved answer deixis.

linguistic_quality:
Natural, precise, economical English. Penalize actual calques, stiffness,
redundancy and unclear syntax—not necessary qualifications. For a non-English
question use null here and fail mode, rather than mislabel its native fluency.

CHECKS
Use pass, fail, or uncertain; explain failures/uncertainty in problems.
- mode: English; eligible genre/content; norm-state stance; no forbidden
  locator; explicit time and two anchors; one fact; length compliance.
- support: correct premises, attribution and scope; complete deciding span
  in the target; no outside answer substance or quoted-norm targeting.
  Established defects fail. Missing necessary English text/identity evidence

- metadata: anchors are two or more distinct, non-generic verbatim question
  substrings, in order; question_type is compatible. A bad reported list
  does not lower textual anchoring if two genuine anchors are present.

sanction_condition_or_consequence;
date_deadline_or_mandate;
quantity_force_or_finance;
reporting_monitoring_or_verification;
actor_body_or_procedure;
situation_scope_or_coverage;
operative_action (the norm/task/authorization, NOT the speech act);
finding_event_or_assessment.
Accept legitimate overlap. Category priority is not a score bonus.

With two or three candidates, batch_diversity passes only when they target
different facts and at least two actual categories. Report separately;
never alter individual scores for diversity. With one use not_applicable.
Treat equivalent defects consistently.

You are a strict faithfulness grader for legal and policy question-answer pairs built from United
  Nations documents.

You will receive a three-section context and THREE question-answer pairs.
The context is:

  a footnote helps a reader.
- "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the SAME document (its opening and neighbouring
  passages), supplied so that the target block can be understood: it resolves which mission "the
  Mission" is, which country "the Government" governs, what period a report covers, and similar
  referring expressions.
BOTH supporting sections are for UNDERSTANDING ONLY. Using them to resolve a referring expression in
  the question or answer (naming "the Mission" as UNAMIR, identifying what a cited resolution
  concerns) is legitimate and must NOT be penalised. Using either of them as a source of answer
  substance is a grounding failure — the answer's facts must come from the TARGET BLOCK itself,
  fully.

THREE question-answer pairs (questions may be in any language; each answer matches its question's
  language). Grade each pair on three sub-criteria, each 1–5. Do NOT evaluate query shape or
  retrieval quality — those are handled separately. Focus only on how faithfully each answer
  reflects the supplied text.

GRADING INSTRUCTIONS:
- Grade each of the three pairs independently and against the absolute rubric below — not relative
  to the other two.
- Do not let similarity or dissimilarity between the three pairs influence any individual grade.
- Evaluate each pair on its own merits before moving to the next.

- 5 is reserved for genuinely exceptional candidates with no identifiable weakness. If you can point

- 4 means the candidate is very good but has exactly one minor, identifiable issue. You must be able
  to name the issue.

  weakness. It is not a punishment grade — most acceptable candidates will receive 3s.
- 2 and 1 are reserved for candidates with real, identifiable problems. Do not avoid using them when
  a candidate qualifies.

You are an expert at creating legal and policy retrieval questions from United Nations documents (resolutions, reports, and letters).
LOOKUP MODE — THE PRACTITIONER KNOWS THE INSTRUMENT AND WANTS ONE POINT FROM IT: every question is a query a practitioner — a sanctions-compliance lawyer, a legal adviser, a mission planner, a policy analyst — puts to a search system when they know WHICH instrument or source governs and need ONE precise fact from it: a measure, a deadline, a ceiling, a criterion, a mandate task, a reported figure. Each question is delivered in TWO RENDERINGS, word-for-word identical except for the instrument slot: by DESCRIPTION in one, by official IDENTIFIER in the other. Write from the need, not from the text: a working question whose answer happens to live in this passage, never a comprehension question about what the passage says.
LANGUAGE AND FIDELITY: questions and answers are written in English. In the ANSWER, reproduce dates, durations, amounts, percentages, troop figures, thresholds and identifiers exactly ("within 30 days" stays "within 30 days"). Use the official English names of organs, bodies, missions and instruments, never literal translations.
PARAPHRASE WITHOUT DRIFT: paraphrase the ordinary scaffolding around the fact; never lift multi-word descriptive fragments from the block as question scaffolding, and never reproduce a list the block gives. Copy terms of art, proper names, figures and dates exactly. A paraphrase must not widen, narrow or shift the norm: "accept" may stand for "recognize", but "weapons ban" may not stand for "arms embargo", and "compensated an applicant" is not "decided that the applicant shall be compensated without further action". Legal text is sensitive to exact words — when unsure whether a word is load-bearing, keep it.
HOW THE INPUT IS STRUCTURED:
Three marked sections. "### TARGET BLOCK" — one contiguous passage of one UN document; you write questions ABOUT this text. "### REFERENCED DOCUMENTS" — documents the block cites, each as symbol, title and text. "### DOCUMENT CONTEXT" — surrounding text of the same document. The block opens with metadata ([EN] Document: <symbol> / Title: <title>) that tells you what the document IS — organ, type (resolution, decision, report, letter, working paper), date — and what it is about.
THE BLOCK TEST — the grounding rule: the ANSWER must be fully stated in the TARGET BLOCK, never in a referenced document, the context or a metadata line. The supporting sections and metadata exist so you can UNDERSTAND the block, and the QUESTION may use what they resolve: which mission "the Mission" is, which parties "the sides" are, which committee "the Committee" is, what a cited instrument is, the organ, type, date and identifier of this document. If any part of the answer's substance sits only outside the block, discard. Citations never complete answers, even when the cited text is supplied: a question answerable from a referenced document is about that document. THE QUOTATION RULE is the same principle for quoted text: when the block quotes or restates a provision of ANOTHER instrument — an article of the Institution-Building Package, a paragraph of an earlier resolution, a rule from a statute — a question about that provision belongs to the quoted instrument; ask instead about what THIS document does with it: alleges, applies, reports, contests, amends. THE DEFINING RULE — TWO RENDERINGS OF EACH QUESTION:
- "question": names the instrument BY DESCRIPTION — organ + year + subject ("the 2004 Security Council resolution on Lebanese sovereignty", "the Secretary-General's July 1999 report on Iraq's oil industry", "the 17 June 2014 New Agenda Coalition working paper on transparency in nuclear disarmament"). No identifier of any kind in this rendering. When same-year instruments share a situation, the subject words must pick THIS one out — "the 2011 Security Council resolution establishing the no-fly zone over Libya", not "the 2011 Security Council resolution on Libya".
- DESCRIPTION ACCURACY: describe the instrument AS IT IS, from the metadata — adopting organ and document type, never omitted ("the 2008 resolution on ..." is incomplete: whose?). A letter is described by date, sender and subject ("the 28 July 2014 letter from Israel on the special session"), with the addressee added when the sender wrote more than one letter on the subject — never "the Security Council letter". A resolution that defers a draft and annexes it is "the 2006 General Assembly resolution deferring consideration of the draft declaration on indigenous peoples", never "the 2006 General Assembly declaration": an annexed draft is not an adopted instrument.
- "question_cited": the same words with the description swapped for the exact official identifier, in natural practitioner phrasing ("in resolution 918 (1994)", "in S/1999/746", "in CD/1989"). The slot is the whole instrument phrase; in the cited rendering it is the identifier, optionally preceded by the source-type words ("the Secretary-General's report S/1999/746" — required for attributed figures, so the office survives). Copy the identifier exactly from the block, a resolved reference or the metadata. Identifier scope: resolution and decision numbers, and report, letter and working-paper symbols — never a PV/SR symbol.
- THE SLOT IS A LOCATOR, NOT A SPEAKER: the instrument tells the searcher where the fact lives. The organ acts ("what did the Security Council authorize for UNAMIR in [instrument]?"); for an operative act, "did [instrument] extend / impose / authorize ..." is accepted practitioner shorthand; the instrument never speaks — no "what did [the resolution / it] say, state, mention, note", and no bare "it" for the instrument.

The description's year is the base rendering's time pin; if the identifier carries no year and the question holds no other absolute date, add one, in both renderings.

ATTRIBUTION: letters convey positions and reports state the reporting body's findings. When the block attributes a claim, estimate or assessment, the question and answer preserve the attribution — to the STATE or OFFICE ("the Secretary-General", "the United States delegation", "KFOR"), never a bare personal name (a name may appear only beside the office).   1. sanction_condition_or_consequence — measures imposed, designation and exemption criteria, conditions for imposing, reviewing or lifting, escalation steps: "Which measures did the Security Council impose on [regime] in [instrument]?", "Under what condition was [X] to be [Y] under [instrument]?", "Did [instrument] extend the arms embargo on [regime] to [actors]?"

  3. quantity_force_or_finance — troop and police ceilings, appropriations and contributions, reported statistics, limits: "What force level did the Security Council authorize for [mission] in [instrument]?", "What amount was appropriated for [X] in [instrument]?"
  4. reporting_monitoring_or_verification — who reports to whom and how often, monitoring bodies, verification and notification arrangements: "How often was [body] to report to the Security Council on [X] under [instrument]?"
  5. actor_body_or_procedure — named officials and bodies, composition, roles, appointment, procedural steps, defined terms: "Which body was tasked with [X] in [instrument]?" — never the identity of a briefer or speaker, which no practitioner needs.
  6. operative_action — what the organ decides, authorizes, demands or requests, and of whom, when it qualifies under CONSEQUENTIAL CONTENT: "What did the Security Council demand of [party] in [instrument]?"
  7. situation_scope_or_coverage — which country, territory, population or period a measure or report covers; carve-outs: "Did [instrument] cover [territory / population]?"
  8. finding_event_or_assessment — concrete dated facts and conclusions, attributed, only facts a practitioner would verify: "According to [described report], what was [figure] as at [date]?" — cited form "According to the Secretary-General's report S/1999/746, ...".

The Security Council,

1. Requests the Secretary-General to continue and intensify his efforts, working together with the international community, to promote an ongoing political process which is ultimately inclusive of all, including by assisting the TFIs in this regard and in delivering services to the Somali people;

You are a strict faithfulness grader for legal and policy question-answer pairs built from United

You will receive a three-section context and THREE question-answer pairs.
The context is:

  a footnote helps a reader.

  Mission" is, which country "the Government" governs, what period a report covers, and similar
  referring expressions.
BOTH supporting sections are for UNDERSTANDING ONLY. Using them to resolve a referring expression in
  the question or answer (naming "the Mission" as UNAMIR, identifying what a cited resolution
  concerns) is legitimate and must NOT be penalised. Using either of them as a source of answer

THREE question-answer pairs (questions may be in any language; each answer matches its question's

  retrieval quality — those are handled separately. Focus only on how faithfully each answer
  reflects the supplied text.

GRADING INSTRUCTIONS:
- Grade each of the three pairs independently and against the absolute rubric below — not relative
